summary: Bellemare and Wichman (February 2019) derive elasticity formulas for the inverse hyperbolic sine (arcsinh) transformation, which approximates a logarithm while retaining zero-valued observations. They cover four specifications (linear-arcsinh, arcsinh-linear, arcsinh-linear with a dummy, and arcsinh-arcsinh) and show with simulations and a re-analysis of the Dehejia and Wahba (1999) NSW data that ad hoc transformations can produce substantially different elasticities. They close with guidelines for applied researchers, including delta-method standard errors and Stata code.
one_line: Derives elasticity formulas for the inverse hyperbolic sine transformation and shows ad hoc transformations can substantially change estimated elasticities.
key_facts: The inverse hyperbolic sine (arcsinh) transformation approximates the natural logarithm and allows retaining zero-valued observations.
The paper was authored by Marc F. Bellemare and Casey J. Wichman and is dated February 24, 2019.
The arcsinh transformation is defined as arcsinh(x) = ln(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1)).
The derivative of arcsinh(x) with respect to x is 1/sqrt(x^2 + 1).
The paper focuses only on nonnegative variables because arcsinh is convex over negative values.
The empirical illustration uses data from Dehejia and Wahba (1999), an evaluation of LaLonde's (1986) National Supported Work (NSW) experiment.
In the NSW data, Earnings78 has 45 zero-valued observations for the treatment group and 92 for the control group.
In the NSW data, 111 treatment and 178 control observations have zero pre-treatment earnings (Earnings75).
In column (1) of Table 3, the NSW program increased post-treatment earnings by $1,750 per year, and the semi-elasticity was approximately 33%.
Using arcsinh on pre-treatment earnings reduced the earnings elasticity from 0.043 to 0.026, a nearly 40 percent reduction.
The paper suggests applying approximate elasticities for values of x or y no less than 10, since values above 10 reduce approximation error to less than half a percent.
Guideline 4 suggests that if a dataset has more than one third zero-valued observations, it is perhaps best to explicitly model selection out of zero, for example with a Tobit or zero-inflated model.
Guideline 6 states that standard errors for these nonlinear elasticity combinations should be obtained using the delta method.
Table 1 simulations show elasticities become more stable as the scaling constant k increases, with virtually no change for k > 10.
